summary: The wall gets built — section by section, gate by gate, by named teams: high priest and goldsmiths, perfumers and district rulers, men and their daughters, one man repairing the stretch 'over against his own house.' Then the enemies mock — a fox could knock this wall down — and Nehemiah answers with prayer.
whyItMatters: This is the chapter that shows the work was real: dozens of named crews, each with a measured stretch. Revival here is not a rally but a roster — ordinary people owning the piece of wall in front of their own house.

context.author: Nehemiah, first-person memoir
context.setting: Jerusalem's circuit wall, roughly two miles, rebuilt in working sections
context.literaryForm: Narrative roster with a closing prayer

keyVerses.text: Then Eliasub the high priest, and his brethren the priests, rose up, and built the sheep-gate; they sanctified it, and set up the doors of it.
keyVerses.why: The first gate built and consecrated is the one through which lambs entered for sacrifice — worship leads the project.

keyVerses.text: And next to him repaired Sallum the son of Alloes, the ruler of half the district round about Jerusalem, he and his daughters.
keyVerses.why: One of the district rulers put his daughters on the wall — the roster quietly records it.

keyVerses.text: Shall not a fox go up and pull down their wall of stones?
keyVerses.why: Tobias's sneer — the wall is a joke to the powerful, which is exactly why finishing it mattered.

keyVerses.text: Hear, O our God, for we have become a scorn; and return thou their reproach upon their head.
keyVerses.why: Nehemiah does not answer the insult in kind; he hands it to God — the first of several such prayers.

questions.question: Why does the Bible spend a whole chapter on a list of names?
questions.answer: Because the list is the point. Each name is a family or guild that owned a section of wall — honor to the workers, a legal record of who restored what, and a standing rebuke to the two men who would not lift a finger. Scripture honors builders by name.

questions.question: Did women really help build the wall?
questions.answer: Yes — Shallum, ruler of half the Jerusalem district, repaired his stretch 'he and his daughters' (13:12). In a roster otherwise full of men and guilds, the daughters are named for their work.

questions.question: Why start with the sheep-gate?
questions.answer: It was the gate where sacrificial lambs entered the temple courts. Building and consecrating it first says something: the point of a secure city is a working altar. The chapter ends where it began — the sheep-gate closes the circuit (13:32).

questions.question: Why does Nehemiah pray for God 'not to cover their iniquity'? Isn't that harsh?
questions.answer: It is an imprecatory prayer — handing justice to God instead of taking revenge. Sanaballat's mockery was an attack on a defenseless community; Nehemiah answers with words to God, not violence against men. Whether we may pray this way is worth sitting with; that he did, and why, is what the text records.

questions.question: Who were the Nathinim mentioned in the list?
questions.answer: Temple servants — a hereditary class of assistants to the Levites, likely descended from the Gibeonites of Joshua 9. They appear in the lists as part of the working community, dwelling in Ophel near the temple.
